facts.fact: A tax deduction reduces the amount of income subject to tax, while a tax credit reduces the tax bill directly, dollar for dollar.
facts.caveat: Some credits are non-refundable and only offset tax owed; a few are refundable. Specifics vary by credit.

facts.fact: In a marginal tax bracket system, higher rates apply only to the portion of income within that bracket, not to all income earned.
facts.caveat: A structural explanation of how brackets work; actual bracket thresholds change annually and by filing status.

facts.fact: Taxpayers can choose between the standard deduction (a flat amount) and itemizing specific deductible expenses, generally picking whichever is larger.
facts.caveat: Exact standard deduction amounts change annually; verify current figures before citing them.

facts.fact: Withholding is an estimate of tax owed collected throughout the year from paychecks; a refund or balance due at filing reflects the difference between withholding and actual tax liability, not a bonus or penalty by itself.
facts.caveat: General mechanics; individual outcomes depend on personal tax situation.

facts.fact: People with significant self-employment or side income in the U.S. may need to pay estimated taxes quarterly rather than relying on employer withholding.
facts.caveat: Thresholds and safe-harbor rules change and depend on individual circumstances; verify current IRS guidance.

facts.fact: Tax-advantaged accounts (like retirement or health savings accounts) can reduce taxable income or grow tax-free/tax-deferred depending on the account type.
facts.caveat: Contribution limits and eligibility rules change annually; verify current figures before citing them.

facts.fact: Filing late without an extension, when taxes are owed, can trigger penalties and interest that generally continue to accrue until the balance is paid.
facts.caveat: Exact penalty rates and structures change; verify current IRS guidance before citing specific percentages.
